How to Deploy Django on AWS (EC2 & RDS) – A Beginner-Friendly Guide [2025]

  • Fixwebsite Issues
  • July 13, 2025
  • 7:04 pm
  • No Comments

Django is one of the most powerful web frameworks for Python developers. But once your app is ready, the big question remains—how do you deploy it so the world can see it? If you’re new to cloud hosting, deploying Django on AWS may sound intimidating. Thankfully, it doesn’t have to be.

In this step-by-step guide, we’ll walk you through everything you need to know to host your Django application on AWS EC2 and RDS—even if you’re just starting out. This guide is tailored to beginners and focuses on practical, real-world deployment.

Table of Contents

Toggle
  • 1. Why Use AWS for Django Deployment?
  • 2. What You’ll Need Before You Begin
  • 3. Step-by-Step: How to Deploy Django on AWS EC2
  • 4. Setting Up AWS RDS for PostgreSQL
  • 5. Configuring Security Groups and Environment Variables
  • 6. Testing and Finalizing Your Deployment
  • 7. Final Thoughts
  • 8. Call to Action

1. Why Use AWS for Django Deployment?

AWS is one of the most reliable, secure, and scalable platforms for hosting web applications. Deploying Django on AWS allows you to:

  • Scale your app easily as traffic grows

  • Store and manage data securely using services like RDS

  • Integrate with other tools (S3 for file storage, CloudFront for CDN, etc.)

  • Customize your server environment with full control via EC2

If you’re serious about taking your Django project to production, AWS is a smart long-term solution.

2. What You’ll Need Before You Begin

Before you start this Django AWS deployment tutorial, make sure you have the following:

  • An AWS account (free tier is fine for testing)

  • A Django project ready for deployment

  • Basic understanding of Linux commands and Python

  • SSH key pair (to access your EC2 instance)

  • PostgreSQL as your database (we’ll use AWS RDS)

This guide will use Ubuntu on EC2, PostgreSQL via AWS RDS, and Gunicorn + Nginx for serving the app.

3. Step-by-Step: How to Deploy Django on AWS EC2

To start deploying your Django app, log in to your AWS Console and navigate to the EC2 section. Launch a new instance using the Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Amazon Machine Image (AMI). Choose the t2.micro instance type, which is included in the AWS free tier. When setting up, select or create a key pair that you’ll use later to connect securely via SSH. Be sure to configure your security group to allow traffic on ports 22 (SSH), 80 (HTTP), and 443 (HTTPS). Once everything is configured, launch the instance and take note of its public IP address.

After launching the instance, you’ll need to connect to it from your local machine using SSH and your key file. Once connected, update the system and install essential packages like Python pip, virtual environment tools, Nginx, and Git. These will help you manage your Django environment and serve your application.

Next, clone your Django project from your repository and navigate into the project directory. Create a Python virtual environment, activate it, and install the required dependencies from your requirements.txt file. At this stage, it’s a good practice to set up a .env file or adjust your Django settings to use environment variables, especially for sensitive information like secret keys and database credentials.

4. Setting Up AWS RDS for PostgreSQL

Now that your EC2 instance is ready, it’s time to set up the database using AWS RDS. Go to the RDS section in the AWS console and create a new PostgreSQL database. Use the free-tier options if you’re testing or in development. Assign your database name, username, and password. Make sure public access is enabled (you can restrict this later) and select the appropriate VPC and subnet group that matches your EC2 configuration. Create a new security group for the RDS instance that allows inbound traffic on port 5432, which is used by PostgreSQL. Configure it so that only your EC2 instance’s IP is allowed to connect. Once your RDS instance is active, return to your Django project and update your database settings to connect to the RDS instance. Use the endpoint provided by AWS, along with the database name, username, and password you set earlier. After updating your settings, run the migration command to apply your database schema to the new PostgreSQL instance.

5. Configuring Security Groups and Environment Variables

For your Django app to function properly, both the EC2 and RDS security groups must allow communication between them. Double-check your configurations in the AWS console to confirm that the EC2 instance can access the RDS instance through the correct port. At the same time, you’ll want to securely manage sensitive settings like your Django secret key and debug mode status. You can do this by setting environment variables either directly in your terminal or by using a .env file combined with a tool like python-decouple or django-environ.

Also, make sure your ALLOWED_HOSTS setting in Django includes your EC2 instance’s public IP address or your custom domain, if you’ve set one up. This ensures Django will respond to requests coming from your live server.

6. Testing and Finalizing Your Deployment

With everything in place, you can now start the Gunicorn server to serve your Django app. Gunicorn acts as a bridge between your Django application and the web server. Once the server is running, you should be able to access your app in the browser by visiting your EC2 public IP on port 8000, confirming that the core deployment is successful.

To make your app production-ready, you’ll need to configure Nginx as a reverse proxy in front of Gunicorn. This allows Nginx to handle incoming requests and forward them to your application efficiently. Create a new server block (or virtual host) configuration file in Nginx to listen on port 80 and direct traffic to Gunicorn on the local machine. After setting up the configuration, enable it and restart Nginx to apply the changes. Once Nginx is running, your Django application will be accessible via the EC2 public IP on the standard web port (port 80). At this point, your app is live and ready to serve users on the internet.

7. Final Thoughts

Deploying a Django app on AWS might seem complex at first, but breaking it down into steps makes it totally manageable—even for beginners. Whether you’re building a portfolio, launching a startup, or deploying client work, AWS offers the tools to grow and scale your Django applications securely.

From EC2 for server hosting to RDS for database management, this setup is both powerful and production-ready. With this guide, you’ve learned how to host Django on AWS EC2, connect it with RDS, and configure everything from Nginx to environment variables.

If you’re serious about deploying Python apps professionally, AWS is a reliable and scalable solution.
